title: The Tool Interface — Why Agents Need Structured I/O
service: ToolLoop: a tool-calling host with a registry, a JSON Schema subset, the four-step loop and a scripted stand-in model

parts.lesson_anchor: The Concept, steps three and four (validate, execute, observe with matching id); Circuit breakers; code/main.py validate and run_loop
planted_bugs: tool_message gives the tool message a fresh uuid instead of the call's id; the KeyError surfaces a turn later, in the scripted model, which reads results by call id
validate accepts True as a number because bool is a subclass of int, so add(a=True, b=2) runs
run_loop uses range(1, max_turns) and gives the model one turn too few, so a request answered on turn 5 is reported as max_turns
Registry keeps a list and scans it in register, get and __contains__, O(n^2) to fill
parts.timing_assert: filling a 7,000-tool registry and a 3,500-tool subset built with get() under 0.04 s (scanning registry 0.7 to 1 s, fixed 0.6 to 2 ms; a fix that leaves get() scanning about 0.15 s)
parts.overfix_guard: a model that never stops calling tools gets exactly max_turns turns and stop=max_turns (no breaker: the stand-in fails on its 101st request); an answer on the last turn reports turns=max_turns, so range(max_turns) counting from 0 fails; calls on the last turn really run; invalid arguments never reach the executor; ints stay numbers; duplicate names still raise ValueError; registration order is kept

parts.lesson_anchor: Step four: observe (the history); 'The result must be serializable'

clarifying_questions: unreadable last line with its newline

an answer with a newline written raw

parts.lesson_anchor: The trust split; Exercise 3 (classify each tool as pure or consequential)
traps: consequential spreads through calls transitively
a diamond lists the shared action once
actions include what a declared consequential tool sets off in turn
the path is the lexicographically smallest, not the declaration order and not the shortest
the first callee by name may be pure

leaves keep their declared kind

a visited set is not a memo

deviations: Part 1: the suggested fourth bug (a consequential tool runs before it is confirmed) was left out. Confirmation belongs to Part 3, and a Part 1 rule that confirms every consequential tool would contradict the Rule of Two, which asks only when all three combine.

Part 1 timing: instead of 2,000 tools times 20,000 dispatches, the test fills a 7,000-tool registry and builds a 3,500-tool subset with get(). Each dispatch through validate and execute costs about 1.5 microseconds in the fixed version, so dispatch timing alone cannot keep 8x margins on both sides within 3 s. Filling the registry plus bare lookups does (0.7 to 1 s against 0.6 to 2 ms), and the 3,500 lookups still catch a fix that leaves get() scanning.

The history includes the assistant message with its tool_calls (the lesson's quiz points out that the lesson's history lacks it), and a tool message's content is the result value itself, not a JSON string, so a NaN reaches the log's serializer.

Part 4: the trace keeps the lesson's line shapes but drops the timing, writes the user message, arguments, results, errors and answer as compact JSON with non-ASCII kept, and merges the lesson's ERROR and VALIDATION ERRORS lines into one ERROR line that carries the error result. The model is async and executors may be async, so the generator has something to await.
Part 5: besides the kind and one explanation path, every tool reports actions, the declared-consequential tools it can reach, sorted and listed once. That is where the diamond is checked.
Part 2 does not test str.splitlines() on U+2028 and U+0085. Chapter 13 already tests that trap in the stdio and transport lessons (07, 09), where newline framing is part of the protocol.
